questions.answer: Critical points occur where \(f_x=0\) and \(f_y=0\). Here \(f_x=2x\) and \(f_y=2y\). Setting these equal to zero gives \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). Therefore the critical point is \((0,0)\).
Compute the first partial derivatives: \(f_x=2x-4\) and \(f_y=2y+6\). Set them equal to zero: \(2x-4=0\) gives \(x=2\), and \(2y+6=0\) gives \(y=-3\). Therefore the only critical point is \((2,-3)\).

Use the second derivative test. We have \(f_{xx}=2\), \(f_{yy}=2\), and \(f_{xy}=0\). The discriminant is \(D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2=2\cdot2-0=4>0\). Since \(f_{xx}>0\), the critical point is a local minimum.

Compute the second derivatives: \(f_{xx}=2\), \(f_{yy}=-2\), and \(f_{xy}=0\). The discriminant is \(D=2(-2)-0^2=-4<0\). A negative discriminant means the point is a saddle point. Therefore \((0,0)\) is a saddle point.

questions.prompt: Find and classify the critical point of \(f(x,y)=x^2+4y^2-2x+8y\).
questions.answer: First find the critical point. \(f_x=2x-2\), so \(x=1\), and \(f_y=8y+8\), so \(y=-1\). For classification, \(f_{xx}=2\), \(f_{yy}=8\), and \(f_{xy}=0\), so \(D=2\cdot8-0=16>0\). Since \(f_{xx}>0\), \((1,-1)\) is a local minimum.
Compute the first partial derivatives: \(f_x=y-1\) and \(f_y=x-1\). Set both equal to zero. From \(y-1=0\), \(y=1\); from \(x-1=0\), \(x=1\). Therefore the only critical point is \((1,1)\).

From the first derivative equations, the critical point is \((1,1)\). The second derivatives are \(f_{xx}=0\), \(f_{yy}=0\), and \(f_{xy}=1\). The discriminant is \(D=0\cdot0-1^2=-1<0\). Therefore \((1,1)\) is a saddle point.

First compute \(f_x=3x^2-3\) and \(f_y=2y\). Setting \(f_y=0\) gives \(y=0\). Setting \(f_x=0\) gives \(3x^2-3=0\), so \(x^2=1\) and \(x=\pm1\). Therefore the critical points are \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\).

The critical points are \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\). Second derivatives are \(f_{xx}=6x\), \(f_{yy}=2\), and \(f_{xy}=0\), so \(D=12x\). At \((1,0)\), \(D=12>0\) and \(f_{xx}=6>0\), so it is a local minimum. At \((-1,0)\), \(D=-12<0\), so it is a saddle point.

questions.prompt: For \(f(x,y)=x^4+y^4\), explain why \((0,0)\) is a local minimum even though the second derivative test is inconclusive.
questions.answer: The first derivatives are \(f_x=4x^3\) and \(f_y=4y^3\), so \((0,0)\) is critical. The second derivatives at \((0,0)\) are all zero, so \(D=0\) and the second derivative test is inconclusive. However \(x^4\ge0\) and \(y^4\ge0\) for all real \(x,y\), so \(f(x,y)=x^4+y^4\ge0=f(0,0)\). Therefore \((0,0)\) is a local minimum.
